claims.text: The initial Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy is in a high-temperature BCC state.
Slow cooling or an intermediate isothermal hold permits local diffusion-driven segregation of Al and Cr.
Al- and Cr-enriched nanoscale clusters or segregation zones form under diffusion-permitting thermal treatments.
Al and Cr preferentially segregate at sites such as grain boundaries or dislocation networks.
Local Al and Cr segregation lowers the free-energy barrier for a phase transition.
The segregation zones act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
The secondary phase may be FCC or an intermetallic phase within or along the boundaries of the BCC matrix.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion sufficiently to prevent formation of Al- and Cr-rich segregation sites.
Rapid quenching therefore retains a predominantly BCC structure.
Slow-cooled or isothermally held samples will contain more secondary phase than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit greater chemical heterogeneity and Al/Cr segregation than rapidly quenched samples.
The secondary-phase fraction will correlate with the measured extent of atomic segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies only when cooling rates or holds provide sufficient time for measurable elemental diffusion.
The mechanism should not apply when cooling is sufficiently rapid to quench the high-temperature state.
Additional alloying, alternative processing, different transformation kinetics, or strain-induced mechanisms may invalidate the proposed segregation mechanism.
The controlled comparison consists of otherwise equivalent samples subjected either to rapid quenching or to slow cooling with an intermediate isothermal hold.
XRD phase quantification and TEM/EDS imaging and mapping can compare phase content, precipitates, and local Al/Cr segregation between the two treatments.
Failure of slow-cooled samples to show a statistically significant increase in secondary-phase content or Al/Cr segregation relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
